format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:
Listen to part of a talk in a materials science class.
Professor: Concrete is the most widely used building material on Earth, but it has a weakness: it cracks. Small cracks may not look serious, but they let water inside. In reinforced concrete, that water can reach the steel bars inside and make them rust. Rusting steel expands, which creates more cracks, and over time the structure weakens. Repairing cracks costs governments enormous amounts of money every year.
So researchers asked an unusual question: what if concrete could repair itself? One of the most interesting solutions uses bacteria. Certain types of bacteria can survive in extreme conditions—they form spores, a kind of sleeping state, and can stay inactive for many years.
Here's how it works. When the concrete is mixed, engineers add these bacterial spores along with food for them—usually a calcium compound such as calcium lactate. As long as the concrete is dry and intact, the spores do nothing. But when a crack forms and water gets in, the spores wake up. They consume the food and produce calcium carbonate—basically limestone—which fills the crack.
This works well for small cracks, generally less than a millimeter wide. It won't fix a broken bridge. And self-healing concrete is more expensive to produce. However, engineers argue that if it reduces repairs over a building's lifetime, the higher starting cost may be worth it.
Let's look at some test results to see how well these materials actually perform.
question: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: Why steel is stronger than concrete
Concrete that uses bacteria to repair its own cracks
How bacteria damage buildings
The history of concrete and why it is the most widely used building material
answer: Concrete that uses bacteria to repair its own cracks
explanation: 細菌を使って自らひび割れを修復するコンクリートが主題。

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:
Listen to part of a talk in a chemistry class.
Professor: Hold up your hands. Your left and right hands are mirror images of each other, but you can't place one perfectly on top of the other—try putting your right hand into a left-handed glove. Many molecules have this same property. We call them chiral, from the Greek word for hand, and the two mirror-image forms are called enantiomers.
In most respects, enantiomers are chemically identical. They have the same boiling point, the same solubility. But in the body, they can behave very differently, because many of the molecules they interact with—enzymes, receptors—are themselves chiral. It's like a handshake: a right hand fits comfortably with another right hand, but not with a left.
The classic illustration is thalidomide, a drug prescribed in the late 1950s, mainly in Europe, to treat morning sickness during pregnancy. It caused severe birth defects in thousands of children. It's often said that one enantiomer was the effective sedative while the other caused the defects—and that if only the "good" form had been sold, the tragedy would have been avoided.
That's a tidy story, but it's misleading. Research later showed that thalidomide's enantiomers convert into each other inside the body. So even a pure dose of one form would quickly become a mixture. The real lessons were about inadequate testing, and the disaster led to much stricter drug regulation.
Still, chirality matters enormously in pharmacology. Today, regulators require companies to study each enantiomer of a new chiral drug separately, and some medicines are sold as a single form.

choices: To check whether students are paying attention
To demonstrate a laboratory safety rule
To give a familiar example of mirror-image objects that cannot be overlapped
To count how many students are present
answer: To give a familiar example of mirror-image objects that cannot be overlapped
explanation: 重ね合わせられない鏡像の身近な例を示すため。

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:
Listen to part of a talk in an urban studies class.
Professor: In 1961, a writer named Jane Jacobs published The Death and Life of Great American Cities. Jacobs wasn't a trained planner—she was a journalist living in Greenwich Village, in New York—but her book became one of the most influential works in urban studies.
At the time, many planners believed that crowded, mixed neighborhoods were unhealthy and chaotic. Their solution was to clear them and build large housing towers surrounded by open space, with homes, shops, and offices kept in separate zones.
Jacobs argued the opposite. She observed her own street closely and concluded that safety came not from police or empty space, but from what she called "eyes on the street." When a street has shops, apartments, and businesses that are busy at different times of day, there are always people around—shopkeepers, residents looking out their windows, people walking by. Their casual attention discourages crime and helps when something goes wrong.
In contrast, the open spaces around many new housing towers were often empty. No one felt responsible for them, and they could become dangerous.
Jacobs also argued for short blocks, buildings of different ages, and density. Old buildings, for instance, offer cheaper rents, which allow small businesses to survive.
Now, critics have pointed out that her ideas were based mainly on a few neighborhoods in New York and may not apply everywhere. And ironically, many of the neighborhoods she praised have since become so popular that ordinary people can no longer afford them. But her emphasis on observing how people actually use streets has shaped planning ever since.
question: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: The history of housing towers in New York
Jane Jacobs's ideas about what makes city neighborhoods work
How police reduced crime in American cities
Why Jane Jacobs became a journalist
answer: Jane Jacobs's ideas about what makes city neighborhoods work
explanation: 都市の近隣がうまく機能する条件についてのジェイン・ジェイコブズの考えが主題。

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:
Listen to part of a talk in a botany class.
Professor: In the fall, in many parts of the world, the leaves on trees turn yellow, orange, and red. Many people think the trees make these colors in the fall. That's partly true, but the story is more interesting.
Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll. Chlorophyll helps the plant use sunlight to make food. This process is called photosynthesis, and it happens mostly in the leaves. But leaves also have yellow and orange colors in them all summer long. We just can't see them, because there is so much green chlorophyll.
In the fall, the days get shorter and colder. The tree gets ready for winter, and it stops making chlorophyll. The green color slowly breaks down. Then the yellow and orange colors, which were there all the time, can finally be seen. So yellow leaves are not new colors—they were hiding!
Red is different. Many trees, like some maples, actually make new red colors in the fall. Scientists are still studying why. One idea is that the red color protects the leaf from too much sunlight while the tree takes useful nutrients back from the leaf before it falls.
Student: So is that why some years the colors are brighter?
Professor: Good question. Yes, the weather matters. Sunny days and cool nights usually make the reds stronger. A very warm, cloudy fall often gives duller colors.
question: What is the main topic of the talk?
choices: How trees make food from sunlight
Why some trees lose their leaves
How maple trees are different from other trees
Why leaves change color in the fall
answer: Why leaves change color in the fall
explanation: 秋に葉の色が変わる理由が主題。

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:
Listen to part of a talk in a climatology class.
Professor: Over the past several decades, the Arctic has warmed far faster than the planet as a whole. Recent analyses suggest that since 1979, it has warmed nearly four times as fast as the global average. Today I want to examine one of the main mechanisms behind this "Arctic amplification": the ice–albedo feedback.
Albedo simply refers to how much incoming sunlight a surface reflects. Fresh snow is extremely reflective, sending back the large majority of the sunlight that hits it. Open ocean, by contrast, is dark and absorbs over ninety percent.
Now consider what happens as the climate warms. Sea ice melts earlier in spring and forms later in autumn. Where bright ice used to sit, there is now dark water. That water absorbs more solar energy, which warms it further, which in turn melts more ice. The process reinforces itself—it's what we call a positive feedback. "Positive" here doesn't mean good; it means the effect amplifies the original change.
I want to be careful, though, not to suggest that albedo explains everything. Other factors contribute substantially—for instance, changes in how heat is transported from lower latitudes, and the fact that the Arctic's lower atmosphere is relatively stable, which traps warming near the surface. In fact, climate models suggest that some amplification would occur even without changes in ice cover, which tells us albedo is a major contributor rather than the sole cause.
The consequences extend beyond the Arctic. There's ongoing debate about whether a warmer Arctic is altering weather patterns farther south, though the evidence there remains contested.
question: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: How sea ice forms in winter
A process that helps explain why the Arctic is warming rapidly
Why the ocean absorbs sunlight
The history of Arctic exploration
answer: A process that helps explain why the Arctic is warming rapidly
explanation: 北極の急速な温暖化を説明する仕組み（氷–アルベド・フィードバック）が主題。

Professor: Today, many people complain that online news is shaped by advertising—that headlines are designed to attract clicks. But this tension is not new. To see where it began, let's go back to New York in 1833.
At the time, most American newspapers cost about six cents—quite expensive for an ordinary worker. They were sold mostly by yearly subscription to merchants and political supporters, and their content focused on business news and party politics.
Then a printer named Benjamin Day launched The Sun, priced at just one penny. How could he sell a paper so cheaply? The key was a new business model. Day relied on advertising, not sales, for most of his income. And advertisers paid according to how many people read the paper. So circulation became everything.
To attract a mass audience, the "penny press" changed what news looked like. Papers sent reporters to police courts, covered crimes and human-interest stories, and were sold on the street by newsboys. Within a few years, The Sun had one of the largest circulations in the country. In 1835, it even published a series of invented stories claiming that life had been discovered on the Moon—and sales soared.
Historians are divided on how to judge the penny press. Some emphasize that it made news available to working people for the first time, and became less tied to political parties. Others point out that the same pressures led to sensationalism. I think both views are right, and that's exactly why it's relevant to debates about digital media today.

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:
Listen to part of a talk in a cognitive science class.
Professor: We tend to assume that if something changes right in front of us, we'll notice. A series of experiments since the 1990s suggests that assumption is badly mistaken. The phenomenon is called change blindness.
The most famous demonstration was conducted by Daniel Simons and Daniel Levin in 1998. A researcher would stop a pedestrian on a college campus and ask for directions. As they talked, two other people carrying a large door walked rudely between them. During the brief moment when the door blocked the pedestrian's view, the original researcher was replaced by a different person—different height, different clothing, different voice. The conversation then simply continued.
Roughly half of the pedestrians failed to notice that they were now talking to someone else entirely.
How can that be? The prevailing interpretation is that our brains don't build a detailed, complete picture of the world from moment to moment. Instead, we encode a fairly sparse representation—the gist of a scene—and rely on the world itself as a kind of external memory. If I need to know what's on the table, I can just look again. This is efficient most of the time, but it means that changes to details we didn't specifically attend to can slip by.
Interestingly, the people who were least likely to notice were often those who saw the researcher as belonging to the same broad category—say, "a student"—as the replacement. That hints that we encode people partly by social category rather than individual features.
Now, it would be a mistake to conclude that perception is simply unreliable. Rather, it's selective, and the selection usually serves us well.

People often fail to notice changes because the brain stores only limited visual detail.
answer: People often fail to notice changes because the brain stores only limited visual detail.
explanation: 脳は視覚の詳細を限られた形でしか保持しないため、変化に気づかないことが多いというのが要点。

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk

Professor: Today, we take the piano for granted. But when it was invented, it solved a real problem for musicians. To understand that problem, we need to look at the instrument that came before it: the harpsichord.
A harpsichord looks a bit like a piano, but inside, when you press a key, a small device plucks the string, a little like a finger plucking a guitar string. The problem is that it plucks the string the same way every time. Whether you press the key gently or hard, the sound is about equally loud. So harpsichord players couldn't easily make one note softer and the next note louder.
Around the year 1700, in Florence, Italy, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori found a solution. Instead of plucking the strings, his instrument struck them with small hammers covered in leather. If you pressed the key harder, the hammer hit the string harder, and the note was louder. Press gently, and it was soft. He called it something like "harpsichord with soft and loud"—in Italian, "piano e forte." That's where our word "piano" comes from.
At first, the new instrument wasn't very popular. It was expensive, and its sound was quieter than people expected. It took decades for composers to really write for it. But by the late 1700s, composers such as Mozart were writing music that depended on those changes between soft and loud.

It could only play a few notes.
answer: Players could not easily control how loud each note was.
explanation: 弦をはじく仕組みのため、音の強弱を変えにくいという問題。

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:
Listen to part of a talk in a marine science class.
Professor: Today I want to answer a simple question: how do whales stay warm? Some whales swim in very cold water, near the ice in the Arctic and the Antarctic. The water there can be colder than zero degrees Celsius. But a whale's body stays at about thirty-six degrees—almost the same as yours. So how do they do it?
The main answer is blubber. Blubber is a thick layer of fat under the skin. In some whales, like the bowhead whale, it can be more than forty centimeters thick. That's about the length of your arm from your elbow to your fingers! Fat does not let heat move through it easily, so blubber works like a warm winter coat.
Blubber has other jobs, too. It stores energy. Many whales eat a lot in the summer, when there is plenty of food in cold waters. Then they travel to warmer places and eat very little for months. During that time, they use the energy in their blubber.
There's one more trick. Whales have special blood vessels in their fins and tails. Warm blood going out passes very close to cold blood coming back. The warm blood heats the cold blood before it returns to the body. So the whale doesn't lose much heat through its thin fins.
Next time, we'll look at how seals, which are much smaller than whales, solve the same problem.

choices: Why whales travel to warmer places
How whales keep their bodies warm in cold water
How whales find food in the Arctic
Why some whales are bigger than others
answer: How whales keep their bodies warm in cold water
explanation: クジラが冷たい水の中で体温を保つ仕組みが主題。

format: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
passage:

Professor: Many Indigenous peoples of North America, including the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois, grew three crops together: corn, beans, and squash. They were often called the "Three Sisters." Today, I want to explain why planting them together worked so well—because it's not just a nice story. There's real science behind it.
First, the corn. Corn grows tall and straight, so it gives the beans something to climb. Bean plants are vines; without support, they spread along the ground.
Second, the beans. Beans have a special relationship with certain bacteria that live on their roots. These bacteria take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form that plants can use. Nitrogen is something corn needs a lot of, so the beans help keep the soil fertile.
Third, the squash. Squash has large, wide leaves that spread across the ground. They shade the soil, which keeps it moist and makes it harder for weeds to grow.
Student: So each plant helps the others?
Professor: Exactly. And there's a nutritional side, too. Corn, beans, and squash together provide a more balanced diet than any one of them alone.
European settlers who arrived later often planted crops in separate rows. Some of them thought the mixed fields looked messy. But researchers who have compared the methods have found that the Three Sisters system can produce more food energy and protein from the same area of land.

choices: How European farming replaced Indigenous methods
How bacteria cause plant diseases
Why growing three crops together was effective
The history of corn in Europe
answer: Why growing three crops together was effective
